title: Putting it into readable words
hook: Tracing paper curls over Ada’s street sketch while one smooth sentence hides the tradeoff.
counterintuition: Readable wording feels like polish. In fact, it is the carrier of earned structure: sequence, contrast, cause, category, or level.
tryThisNow: Choose one sentence and write its relationship in the margin: sequence, contrast, cause, or category. Revise only to make that relationship visible.
keyTakeaway: Readable words should copy the structure image faithfully, so the reader receives the relationship without rebuilding it silently.

breakdown.fastRead:
Tracing paper curls over Ada's crosswalk sketch and bus-lane diagram. Her public notice says the street will be improved for all users. It is smooth and useless. She sketches the tradeoff first: protected crossings before faster buses at the curb. Then she writes a sentence that keeps the before-after street image intact.

Readable words are not nicer words. They are structure carried cleanly. First create the image of what the logic is doing. Then copy that image in words so sequence, contrast, and cause do not blur.
breakdown.deepRead:
What has to happen first for the battery result to make sense? Jonas asks with a thermal test graph, a failure threshold note, and an investor update open on the lab table. His first sentence jumps from result to claim. Investors would hear confidence without seeing the path.

He draws the image: test begins, heat rises, threshold is crossed, cell fails. Then he writes the sentence in that order.

The sentence can only copy the image if the writer has first seen what the structure is doing. If the structure is sequence, the wording should move in sequence. If it is contrast, the sentence should preserve the difference. If it is cause, the cause should not disappear into a vague label.

Smoothness can be a trap. A sentence can sound calm while hiding the relationship the reader needs.

Readable expression translates structure. It does not replace structure. The task is not softer wording. The sentence has to deliver the relationship intact.

Test the sentence against the picture you meant to build. If the picture has one main branch and three supports, the words should give the reader that same path without asking them to infer it.
breakdown.fullRead:
Isabel learned the cost of smoothness from three angry patron replies. Her festival policy note said the new ticket tiers improve access while sustaining programming. The seating chart and ticket-tier table told a more precise story: cheaper balcony seats were protected before premium orchestra prices rose. The original sentence had erased that order and made the change sound like a price grab.

She rewrote it with the structure visible: balcony access stays protected; orchestra prices rise to fund it. The sentence was not prettier in any decorative sense. It was more faithful.

Readable words are successful when the reader receives the architecture without having to rebuild it silently. That is the final job after grouping, ordering, problem solving, and summary precision. A sentence should not blur the very relationship the structure worked so hard to earn.

Take a sentence you like and ask what relationship it carries. Is it showing before and after, cause and effect, contrast, category, or sequence? If you cannot answer, the sentence may be fluent without being readable in the useful sense.

Marco faces the same test on a cloud outage status page. The smooth phrase service instability hides the path: a failed certificate renewal caused authentication failures, which triggered recovery work. Customers do not need ornamental detail. They need enough cause and recovery order to trust the update. Marco replaces instability with the sequence the logs show.

Chiara uses the method under pressure at a legal clinic. Tenants reading an eviction leaflet do not have spare attention. She draws notice, deadline, response, and hearing as four boxes on a yellow legal pad, then writes the leaflet sentence so the boxes stay in order. The legal exceptions remain, but they no longer collapse into one dense paragraph.

There is a limit. Structure-faithful wording is not permission to make sentences heavy. If every relationship is overexplained, the reader still works too hard. The right sentence carries the relationship with the least friction that keeps it true.

Ryan's warranty postmortem makes the category version plain. One pleasant paragraph had blended crash damage, ordinary wear, and manufacturer defects. Customers and staff argued because the language had blurred categories the policy needed to keep separate. Ryan rewrote the paragraph as three category sentences. Less elegant, more useful.

The final test is simple. Can the reader see the same image you saw before writing the sentence? If yes, the words have done their job. If not, polish has become a substitute for structure, and the sentence needs to be rebuilt from the image outward.

To create the image is to see the logic pattern before polishing the line. To copy the image in words is to make the language carry that architecture without asking the reader to rebuild it silently.

examples.title: Ada Keeps the Street Tradeoff Visible

planSpec.domain: an urban-design studio led by Ada writing a public note about street changes
planSpec.audience: planners turning structural reasoning into readable prose
planSpec.stakes: residents will misunderstand tradeoffs if contrast and sequence blur into planning language
planSpec.requiredBeat: Ada sketches the tradeoff first, then writes one sentence that keeps the before-after street image intact instead of hiding it behind improvement language.

examples.scenario: Ada watches tracing paper curl over a crosswalk sketch and a bus-lane diagram in the urban-design studio. The public notice draft says the corridor will improve mobility for everyone. Before the neighborhood mailing goes out, Ada faces a choice: keep the smooth phrase or preserve the tradeoff. She sketches protected crossings before curbside bus priority, then writes one sentence that keeps the street image intact.
examples.whatToDo: Name the before-after street relationship in the sentence. Keep the protected crossing and bus-lane tradeoff visible instead of hiding it behind improvement language.
examples.whyItMatters: Residents need to understand what changes and in what order. A smooth promise blurs the physical tradeoff the drawing already shows.

examples.title: Jonas Writes the Battery Test in Order

planSpec.domain: a materials scientist explaining a battery-test sequence to investors
planSpec.audience: technical founders making complex sequence readable
planSpec.stakes: investors will confuse cause and sequence if the sentence jumps from result to claim without the test path
planSpec.requiredBeat: Jonas asks what image the sentence must carry, draws test, heat rise, failure threshold, and result, then writes the sequence in that order.

examples.scenario: What has to happen first for the battery result to make sense? Jonas asks beside a thermal test graph and a failure threshold note. The investor update jumps from failure result to market claim, and the founders like how confident it sounds. Jonas must decide whether confidence is enough. He draws the image: test, heat rise, threshold, result. Then he writes the sentence in that order.
examples.whatToDo: Put the test sequence into the sentence: test condition, heat rise, threshold crossing, result. Do not skip the path to sound decisive.
examples.whyItMatters: Investors need cause and sequence, not a leap from result to claim. The sentence should carry the test image they cannot see.

examples.title: Isabel Restores the Seat-Access Order

planSpec.domain: a classical-music festival explaining ticket-tier changes
planSpec.stakes: patrons will hear a price grab unless the sentence preserves the relationship between access and seat allocation
planSpec.requiredBeat: Isabel replaces vague affordability language with a sentence that shows cheaper balcony seats are protected before premium orchestra prices rise.

examples.scenario: As the ticketing director in the patron services office, Isabel needed three angry draft replies to see the sentence had erased the structure. The seating chart protected balcony seats, and the ticket-tier table raised premium orchestra prices, but the patron email draft said affordability improvements. After patrons read that as a price grab, Isabel rewrote the sentence: cheaper balcony seats stay protected before premium orchestra prices rise.
examples.whatToDo: Write the access relationship directly. Show protected balcony seats before premium orchestra increases so readers see what funds what.
examples.whyItMatters: Patrons judge fairness from the relationship between access and price. Vague affordability wording erases the order that makes the policy defensible.

examples.title: Marco Restores Cause on the Status Page

planSpec.domain: a cloud-infrastructure lead named Marco writing outage language for customers
planSpec.audience: technical leaders translating cause and recovery clearly
planSpec.stakes: customers will lose trust if the prose sounds smooth but hides the causal path of the outage
planSpec.requiredBeat: "Do not call it instability if the cause was a failed certificate renewal," Marco says, then rewrites the sentence to preserve cause, failure, and recovery order.

examples.scenario: "Do not call it instability," Marco says as the incident lead in the operations room while the status page clock keeps counting. The certificate renewal log and recovery timeline sit beside the customer update. A teammate wants the smooth line, some users experienced service instability. Marco has to choose between calm wording and causal order. He rewrites it: a failed certificate renewal blocked authentication, then recovery restored access.
examples.whatToDo: Preserve cause, failure, and recovery order in the status sentence. Use plain terms, but do not blur the causal path into instability.
examples.whyItMatters: Customers trust a clear path more than a smooth label. If cause disappears, the update sounds evasive even when the recovery work is real.

examples.title: Chiara Keeps the Four Legal Boxes in Order

planSpec.domain: a community legal clinic writing an eviction-rights leaflet
planSpec.audience: public legal educators making structure readable under stress
planSpec.stakes: tenants may miss the action sequence if legal exceptions are smoothed into one dense paragraph
planSpec.requiredBeat: You watch Chiara draw notice, deadline, response, and hearing as four boxes, then write the leaflet sentence so the boxes stay in order.

examples.scenario: You are holding a draft leaflet beside four boxes drawn on a yellow legal pad at the community legal clinic. Chiara has a notice deadline chart and hearing response form open. The old paragraph blends exceptions, deadlines, and hearing rights into one dense block. Before the leaflet is printed, Chiara has to choose structure over smoothness. She writes notice, deadline, response, and hearing in that order.
examples.whatToDo: Write the sentence so the four boxes stay in sequence: notice, deadline, response, hearing. Keep exceptions attached to the step they modify.
examples.whyItMatters: Tenants under stress need action order. A smooth paragraph can hide the deadline sequence and make legal rights harder to use.

examples.title: Ryan Splits the Warranty Paragraph

planSpec.domain: a specialty cycling shop explaining warranty exclusions
planSpec.audience: retail owners writing customer policies without blurring categories
planSpec.stakes: customers and staff will argue if crash damage, wear, and manufacturer defects are not linguistically separated
planSpec.requiredBeat: At 10:40 a.m., Ryan turns one pleasant warranty paragraph into three category sentences that preserve the structure customers need to compare.

examples.scenario: At 10:40 a.m., Ryan lays a cracked carbon rim beside the warranty card on the cycling shop service counter. The service counter form has one pleasant paragraph about exclusions, and staff keep arguing with customers. In the postmortem, Ryan separates crash damage, ordinary wear, and manufacturer defects into three category sentences. The paragraph becomes less charming and far clearer.
examples.whatToDo: Split the warranty paragraph into crash damage, ordinary wear, and manufacturer defect categories. Let each sentence preserve one category.
examples.whyItMatters: Customers and staff need comparable categories. Pleasant language that blends them creates arguments at the counter.

questions.prompt: A public notice says a street change will improve mobility for everyone, but the real structure is protected crossings before bus-lane priority. What should the sentence do?
choices: Preserve the before-after tradeoff in plain words.
Use friendlier language about community benefits.
Remove all details to avoid conflict.
questions.explanation: Readable wording should carry the structure. The tradeoff is the key image; friendlier language or fewer details would blur it.

questions.prompt: A battery update jumps from failed test to investment claim without showing heat rise and threshold crossing. What is missing?
choices: A longer market forecast.
More adjectives about performance.
The sequence that lets readers follow cause and result.
questions.explanation: The missing element is structural sequence. Investors need the path from test to result before weighing the claim.

questions.prompt: A festival policy says affordability improvements, but the actual structure protects balcony seats before raising orchestra prices. What revision fits?
choices: Keep the phrase because it is positive.
State the protected seats and price increase relationship directly.
Delete all mention of prices., while preserving the same order that made the argument hard to judge
questions.explanation: The sentence should preserve the access-price relationship. Positive wording hides the structure patrons need to judge fairness.

questions.prompt: A status page says service instability, but logs show a failed certificate renewal caused authentication failures before recovery. What should the update do?
choices: Avoid cause because customers dislike technical detail.
Use a softer word than failure.
Preserve cause, failure, and recovery order.
questions.explanation: Plain language can still show causal order. Hiding cause in a vague label sounds evasive and weakens trust.

questions.prompt: A legal leaflet blends notice, deadline, response, and hearing in one dense paragraph. What is the best readability repair?
choices: Add encouraging language before the paragraph.
Keep the action sequence visible and attach exceptions to the right step.
Move hearing rights into a footnote., while postponing the actual test the material needs to pass
questions.explanation: Tenants need sequence under stress. Readability means the action path stays visible, not that the paragraph sounds warmer.

questions.prompt: A warranty policy blends crash damage, wear, and manufacturer defects into one pleasant paragraph. Why does splitting it help?
choices: It preserves categories customers and staff need to compare.
It makes the shop sound more formal.
It may reduce support calls by making policy categories easier to explain.
questions.explanation: The split carries category structure. Formality and claim volume are not the point; the policy needs categories that do not blur.

questions.prompt: A sentence sounds smooth, but the writer cannot say whether it carries contrast, sequence, cause, or category. What is the likely problem?
choices: It is probably too short.
It may be fluent without transmitting structure.
It should use more technical vocabulary.
questions.explanation: Fluency alone is not enough. If the relationship cannot be named, the sentence may make the reader rebuild the structure silently.

questions.prompt: A writer overexplains every relationship until the sentence becomes heavy. What boundary should guide revision?
choices: Carry the relationship with the least friction that keeps it true.
Rethink the underlying relationship, because heavy overexplanation may mean the structure itself is not clear enough yet.
Use the longest sentence for complex ideas.
questions.explanation: Readable wording should preserve structure without excess weight. Deleting the relationship or making it long by default misses the balance.

questions.prompt: A team has finished the structure for a customer notice and asks whether the wording should now be made smoother before release. What is the strongest standard for improving the sentence?
choices: Make the prose pleasant enough that readers like the tone.
Shorten every sentence by at least half.
Copy the structure image in words so readers receive the relationship.
questions.explanation: The standard is structural transmission. Pleasant tone and short sentences help only when they preserve the relationship already earned.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean to create the image before writing?
reviewCards.back: See the relationship the sentence must carry: sequence, contrast, cause, category, or level. Then choose words that preserve that image.

reviewCards.front: Why can smooth wording be dangerous?
reviewCards.back: It can hide the structure readers need. A calm phrase may blur cause, sequence, or category and force readers to rebuild the logic themselves.

reviewCards.front: A sentence hides cause under a vague label. What is the repair?
reviewCards.back: Name the cause and the result in order, using plain words. Do not trade trust for a smoother label.

reviewCards.front: How do you revise a dense action sequence?
reviewCards.back: Draw the steps first, then write the sentence so the steps remain in order. Attach exceptions or details to the step they modify.

reviewCards.front: What is the final readability test?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the reader can see the same structure image you saw before writing. If not, rebuild the sentence from the relationship outward.

implementationPlan.title: Copy the Structure Image
implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to make wording accountable to structure. The skill is seeing the relationship before revising the sentence, then carrying that relationship in plain language without blurring it.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a sentence says improve, then ask what concrete before-after relationship it hides and rewrite that relationship plainly.
If cause and recovery matter, then write them in order even if a smoother label is available.
If readers must act in sequence, then draw the boxes first and write the sentence in that order.
If categories keep getting argued about, then split the sentence by category instead of smoothing them together.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one sentence and write its relationship in the margin: sequence, contrast, cause, or category. Revise only to make that relationship visible.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, pick three sentences from important writing. For each, name the structure image it should carry and revise one that sounds fluent but hides the relationship.

memorableLines.text: Readable words are not nicer words.
memorableLines.why: It rejects the common style-polish misread.

memorableLines.text: A sentence can sound calm while hiding the relationship the reader needs.
memorableLines.why: It explains why fluency alone can damage readability.

memorableLines.text: Can the reader see the same image you saw before writing the sentence?
memorableLines.why: It states the closing readability test as a reusable question.
